title: The true good
hook: the good belongs to reason, not to the senses (Letters 124)

segments.voice: Yesterday: plain bread, dry and delicious to a hungry man. Your line was hunger is the sauce. What tasted better than you expected? Day four hundred ninety, the end of a week.

A puppy rolls in the grass in the sun. It's warm, fed, scratched behind the ears. Is it having a good life? The obvious answer is yes. Letter 124 says something stranger. This is the last of Seneca's letters to Lucilius that survive, and he ends not with a goodbye but with an argument. How do we know what's good? Do we feel it, the way the puppy feels the sun? Or do we understand it? His answer sounds cold at first. Stay with it to the end. Today: the true good.
screen: `A PUPPY IN THE SUN.` → `THE LAST LETTER THAT SURVIVES.` → `FELT, OR UNDERSTOOD?`

segments.voice: First, the question. The rival school of Epicurus said the good is pleasure, and pleasure is judged by the senses. Seneca disagrees. The senses, he says, can tell you warm from cold, sweet from bitter. They can't tell you what's worth doing. That's the job of reason. Second, the puppy and the baby. Seneca goes further. An animal, or an infant who can't yet reason, can be healthy, lively, comfortable. But the full good, in the Stoic sense, belongs only to a creature that can understand and choose. He isn't saying the puppy doesn't matter. He's saying its kind of good is a different thing from the good of a person who chooses well. Third, why this frees you. If the good were pleasure, then anyone who controls your comfort would control your good. A bad night's sleep would ruin it. Seneca's good lives in reason, which means it lives in what you choose to do with the night you got. Fourth, the letters end mid-conversation. We lose the trail here. An ancient writer, Aulus Gellius, quotes from a later book of the letters, so there were once more. They're gone. Seneca's last surviving word to his friend is an argument, still going. And our week, looking back: learn to live, try it, rich in enough, under the gold, with the sun, hunger is the sauce. Every one of those is reason's good, chosen over what the senses wanted first.
screen: `THE SENSES FEEL; REASON JUDGES.` · `THE PUPPY'S GOOD AND A PERSON'S GOOD.` · `GOOD THAT NO BAD NIGHT CAN TAKE.` · `THE LETTERS STOP MID-ARGUMENT.` · then, large: `REASON'S GOOD.`

segments.voice: Think of one choice coming up today where craving and reason pull different ways. Another coffee or water. Snapping back or waiting. Buying or not. Let craving speak first. Hear it out fully: what it wants, how good it would feel. Then let reason speak, slowly: what would you choose if you could see the whole day from the evening? You don't have to decide yet. Just notice that you are the one who listens to both. The bell holds the time.
Ratio. Latin for reason: Seneca's last surviving letter says the true good lives not in what the senses feel, but in what reason understands and chooses. Today's word.
Your line: reason's good. Make the choice you just pictured, and make it by reason. Afterward, notice whether the good stayed with you longer than the craving would have. Day four hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners pause before a choice to separate what the senses want from what reason judges good, following the teaching Seneca sets out in Letter 124.

fork.setup: you're an Epicurean arguing with Seneca. you say the good is pleasure, judged by the senses. what does he answer?
options: the senses can't judge what's worth doing; reason does.
fork.reveal: Seneca says the senses report warm and sweet, but only reason can tell what is good.

original.note: Latin, 'reason': where Seneca says the true good lives.

what it means: for Seneca the good is understood and chosen by reason, not felt by the senses.
what a scholar hears: the collection breaks off at Letter 124; Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 12.2, quotes from a 22nd book of the letters, so at least some were lost.

notes: Letters 124 paraphrased: whether the good is grasped by the senses or the intellect; the senses judge only present sensations; animals and infants lack the perfect good because they lack reason. Confirm the framing, especially the fairness line about animals.
